revisions.title: A bounded permission to examine the laws
revisions.body: Before discussing defects in their cities’ laws, the Athenian tests whether age and the absence of young people make this conversation permitted. The answer is yes: the elders may speak alone. This frames the criticism as a bounded dramatic procedure, not a general invitation.

revisions.title: From persuasive myth to an age rule
revisions.body: The Sidonian tale is introduced as an improbable but persuasive paradigm for the lawgiver. The Athenian then turns to a concrete age rule: children are kept from wine; younger adults drink moderately; men over forty may call on Dionysus at symposia to soften old age and make their souls pliable. The proposal gives older participation in song a civic setting.

revisions.title: From private wish to wiser prayer
revisions.body: The Athenian begins with a wish shared by everyone: that things follow the command of one’s own soul. Megillus then redirects the object of prayer and striving toward phronesis and nous, for the city and for each person. The movement is from getting what one wants to wanting what intelligence can guide.

revisions.title: A layered report of constitutional safeguards
revisions.body: The Athenian recounts Sparta’s constitutional balance as a layered report: a god gives kingship twin birth; human nature mixed with divine power adds the council of elders; a third saviour adds the ephors as a bridle. The sequence is presented as a report of how successive powers were mixed into the rule.

revisions.title: Persia and the education of successors
revisions.body: The Persian example contrasts political moderation with inherited upbringing. Under Cyrus, shared speech and counsel are said to accompany flourishing; his sons, however, are raised as already blessed, with no one allowed to oppose them. The passage directs attention from a ruler’s ancestry to the education that forms successors.

revisions.title: Honor must make the soul better
revisions.body: The speech gives honor a practical test: a soul is not honored by speeches, gifts, or concessions unless they make it better. Self-praise that leaves conduct unchecked is likewise called harm rather than honor. I hear the passage redirecting honor from appearance to formation.

revisions.title: Praise and blame prepare the hearer
revisions.body: Before statutes are stated, the Athenian assigns praise and blame a preparatory task: they make people more tractable and well-disposed toward the coming laws. The hinge is a change of register—from setting laws down to shaping the hearer’s disposition toward them.

revisions.title: Purification becomes a legislative problem
revisions.body: The Athenian distinguishes this founding from a colony or a selection by purification. Instead, many streams flow into one lake, and the legislator must keep the inflowing water as pure as possible by drawing some off, channeling others, and diverting the rest. Purification becomes an active legislative problem.

revisions.title: The lawgiver’s rule for approximation
revisions.body: The Athenian distinguishes a model from its implementation. A lawgiver should display the finest and truest pattern, but when an element proves impossible, omit that element and devise the closest fitting remainder. The standard is deliberate approximation, not a claim that every detail can be enacted.

revisions.title: Different disputes, different procedures
revisions.body: The city does not place every dispute in a single court. Private appeals go to a common court whose judges are selected by the offices; public indictments begin and end with the people while three high offices examine; tribal courts use jurors chosen by lot for private cases. The point is differentiated procedure.

revisions.title: Justice is tested in treatment of slaves
revisions.body: The passage turns a dispute about what to say of slaves into a test of conduct. One maxim praises slaves as potentially excellent; another treats the class as untrustworthy. The Athenian then makes conduct toward slaves—the people easiest to wrong—the measure of genuine justice. Reverence for justice must show itself in treatment.
